points: Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms is commonly known as the notwithstanding clause.
The clause is called « clause dérogatoire » in French.
The clause is also called « clause nonobstant » in French.
The Parliament of Canada may invoke the notwithstanding clause.
Provincial legislatures may invoke the notwithstanding clause.
Territorial legislatures may invoke the notwithstanding clause.
The notwithstanding clause can temporarily override section 2 and sections 7 through 15 of the Charter.
Under subsection 33(1), a declaration must expressly state the override in an Act.
A declaration can cover an entire Act.
A declaration can cover individual provisions of an Act.
A declaration can override one or more provisions within the eligible Charter sections.
Under subsection 33(2), a law covered by an active declaration operates as it would if the Charter provision named in the declaration did not apply.
Under subsection 33(3), a declaration expires five years after it comes into force unless it specifies an earlier expiry date.
Under subsection 33(4), a legislature may re-enact a declaration.
Under subsection 33(5), a re-enacted declaration is subject to the same expiry rule as the original declaration.
The notwithstanding clause cannot be invoked by implication.
The law invoking the clause must clearly identify which Charter rights it overrides.
Invoking the clause requires no special legislative procedure.
A bill invoking the clause goes through the ordinary legislative process.
A bill invoking the clause requires only a simple majority, like any other bill.
A legislature can use a separate omnibus statute to invoke the clause.
An omnibus declaration can identify one or more laws that will operate going forward despite the specified Charter rights.
Normally, a law's validity can be challenged in court on the ground that it infringes a Charter right.
Under section 1 of the Charter, a court can uphold a law that infringes a Charter right if the infringement is justified in a free and democratic society.
Invoking the notwithstanding clause prevents courts from reviewing a law's compliance with the Charter rights specified in the declaration.
Section 2 protects fundamental freedoms.
Sections 7 through 14 protect legal rights.
Section 15 protects equality rights.
Section 2 protects freedom of expression.
Section 2 protects freedom of religion.
Section 2 protects freedom of thought.
Section 2 protects freedom of belief.
Section 2 protects freedom of peaceful assembly.
Section 2 protects freedom of association.
The Charter's legal rights include the right to life.
The Charter's legal rights include the right to liberty.
The Charter's legal rights include the right to security of the person.
The Charter's legal rights protect against unreasonable search and seizure.
The Charter's legal rights protect against arbitrary detention or imprisonment.
The Charter's legal rights include the right to legal counsel.
The Charter's legal rights guarantee habeas corpus.
The Charter's rights in criminal and penal matters include the presumption of innocence until proven guilty.
The Charter's legal rights protect against cruel and unusual punishment.
The Charter's legal rights protect against self-incrimination.
The Charter's legal rights include the right to an interpreter in court proceedings.
Section 15 protects against discrimination by the government.
The notwithstanding clause does not apply to mobility rights under section 6.
The notwithstanding clause does not apply to democratic rights under sections 3 through 5.
The notwithstanding clause does not apply to language rights under sections 16 through 23.
The notwithstanding clause does not apply to the enforcement provision in section 24.
The notwithstanding clause does not apply to the sexual equality provision in section 28.
The five-year expiry limit matches the maximum term of Parliament or a legislature before an election must be called.
The five-year limit gives voters a chance to hold elected officials accountable for invoking the clause.
Voters who oppose a law can elect representatives who can repeal it.
Voters who oppose a declaration can elect representatives who can let it expire rather than renew it.
The notwithstanding clause reflects the hybrid nature of Canadian political institutions.
The clause preserves an element of the British tradition of parliamentary supremacy.
Canada introduced an American-style system of written constitutional rights and strong courts in 1982.
Former prime minister Jean Chrétien portrayed the clause as a safeguard against a hypothetical Supreme Court ruling protecting hate speech as freedom of expression.
Chrétien also portrayed the clause as a safeguard against a hypothetical Supreme Court ruling protecting child pornography as freedom of expression.
Pierre Trudeau became prime minister in 1968.
After becoming prime minister, Trudeau advocated patriating the Canadian Constitution.
After becoming prime minister, Trudeau advocated adopting a constitutional bill of rights.
Several efforts to patriate the Constitution with a bill of rights failed in the 1970s.
The Victoria Charter was among the failed efforts.
Trudeau announced plans for a constitutional bill of rights that would include fundamental freedoms.
Freedom of movement was among the freedoms Trudeau proposed to include.
Trudeau's proposal included democratic guarantees.
Trudeau's proposal included legal rights.
Trudeau's proposal included language rights.
Trudeau's proposal included equality rights.
Trudeau's proposal gained popular support.
The Progressive Conservative opposition opposed Trudeau's proposal.
The 1981 Patriation Reference accelerated the patriation process.
In the Patriation Reference, the Supreme Court of Canada affirmed that the federal government could legally patriate the Constitution unilaterally.
In the Patriation Reference, the Supreme Court recognized a constitutional convention that some provincial approval should be sought for constitutional reform.
Alberta Premier Peter Lougheed proposed including the notwithstanding clause in the Charter.
Alberta passed the Alberta Bill of Rights in 1972.
The Alberta Bill of Rights included its own notwithstanding clause.
Alberta Attorney General Merv Leitch suggested including a notwithstanding clause in the Alberta Bill of Rights.
The Charter's notwithstanding clause was a compromise reached during the constitutional debate of the early 1980s.
A major provincial objection was that the Charter shifted power from elected officials to the judiciary.
The provinces objected that this shift would give the courts the final word.
Section 33 was intended to give provincial legislators more leverage to pass laws.
The section 1 limitations clause was also intended to give provincial legislators more leverage to pass laws.
Trudeau initially strongly objected to the notwithstanding clause.
Trudeau eventually agreed to include the clause under pressure from provincial premiers.
The clause was included as part of the Kitchen Accord.
The constitutional conference that produced the Kitchen Accord was close to ending in deadlock.
Jean Chrétien was the federal justice minister during the Kitchen Accord negotiations.
Roy McMurtry was a provincial minister during the negotiations.
Roy Romanow was a provincial minister during the negotiations.
Chrétien, McMurtry, and Romanow laid the groundwork for a deal in a kitchen at the Government Conference Centre in Ottawa.
One of the two major changes to the constitutional package was the inclusion of the notwithstanding clause in the Charter.
The other major change was agreement on a formula for amending the Constitution.
The negotiators worked through the night.
The negotiators consulted different premiers.
The deal secured agreement from almost everyone.
René Lévesque, the premier of Quebec, was excluded from the negotiations.
Lévesque refused to agree to the deal.
The Quebec government declined to endorse the constitutional amendment.
Chrétien later said Canada probably would not have had a Charter without the notwithstanding clause.
In exchange for agreeing to the clause, Trudeau declined to remove the federal power of disallowance from the draft Constitution.
In exchange for agreeing to the clause, Trudeau declined to remove the federal power of reservation from the draft Constitution.
When the clause was introduced, there were concerns that governments could abuse it.
Alan Borovoy was the general counsel of the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.
Borovoy argued that the political difficulty of invoking the clause was a reasonable safeguard for the Charter.
According to Chrétien, Trudeau blamed him for the notwithstanding clause in 1992.
Chrétien replied that he had recommended the clause but that Trudeau had agreed to give it to the provinces.
The party leaders' debate for the 2006 federal election took place on January 9, 2006.
At the debate, Prime Minister Paul Martin unexpectedly pledged that a re-elected Liberal government would support a constitutional amendment barring the federal government from invoking section 33.
Martin challenged Conservative leader Stephen Harper to agree to the proposal.
Martin's pledge sparked debate over which procedure would be needed to amend the clause.
Some argued that Martin's proposal required the standard procedure, including approval from at least seven provinces.
Under that procedure, the approving provinces would have to represent at least half of the national population.
Others argued that Parliament could make the change alone because it would limit only the federal Parliament's powers.
Constitutional scholar Peter Hogg described the notwithstanding clause as seemingly a uniquely Canadian invention.
The U.S. Constitution gives the states no equivalent override power.
Article III, section 2 of the U.S. Constitution authorizes Congress to remove jurisdiction from the federal courts.
According to the article, Congress has not assembled the necessary majority to exercise that power since World War II.
The concept of a notwithstanding clause predates the Canadian Charter.
The Canadian Bill of Rights dates to 1960.
Section 2 of the Canadian Bill of Rights allows an Act of Parliament to declare that a law operates notwithstanding that Bill of Rights.
The Canadian Bill of Rights override can apply to any right under that instrument, unlike the Charter override, which is limited to specified sections.
The Saskatchewan Human Rights Code of 1979 contains a similar device.
The Quebec Charter of Human Rights and Freedoms of 1977 contains a similar device.
Israel added a similar device to one of its Basic Laws in 1992.
The Israeli override could be used only with respect to freedom of occupation.
Israel's proposed 2023 judicial reform envisaged extending the override to all matters.
The proposed Israeli extension would have covered Basic Laws that do not deal with rights and freedoms.
Section 31 of the Victorian Charter of Human Rights and Responsibilities serves a similar purpose in Victoria, Australia.
The United Kingdom's uncodified constitution has an implicit equivalent of a notwithstanding clause.
Under UK parliamentary sovereignty, the courts cannot invalidate primary legislation on constitutional grounds.
UK courts cannot invalidate primary legislation because it is incompatible with the European Convention on Human Rights.
The UK's Human Rights Act 1998 requires legislation to be interpreted compatibly with the European Convention on Human Rights where possible.
UK courts must enforce primary legislation even if they cannot interpret it compatibly with the Convention.
Incompatible secondary legislation in the UK may be beyond the enacting body's powers.
Incompatible devolved legislation in the UK may be beyond the enacting body's powers.
Four provinces have passed laws invoking the notwithstanding clause.
One territory has passed a law invoking the notwithstanding clause.
Quebec has invoked the notwithstanding clause more often than any other jurisdiction.
Quebec applied the clause across all its laws from 1982 to 1985.
Quebec used the clause for a French-only sign law in 1988.
Quebec used the clause in 2019 for a law prohibiting state-affiliated employees from wearing religious symbols.
Quebec used the clause in 2022 for a law strengthening the use of French.
Saskatchewan passed strike-breaking legislation invoking the clause in 1986.
Saskatchewan passed another law invoking the clause in 2018.
The 2018 Saskatchewan law would have allowed the government to pay for non-Catholics to attend publicly funded Catholic schools.
The 2018 Saskatchewan law was never brought into force.
Ontario passed a law invoking the clause in 2021 to lengthen the pre-election period during which third-party groups had to limit their activities.
Yukon invoked the clause in 1982.
Yukon's 1982 law invoking the clause was never brought into force.
The federal government has never invoked the notwithstanding clause.
Alberta introduced a bill concerning past forced sterilizations in 1998.
The bill sought to use the notwithstanding clause to limit lawsuits against the Alberta government.
The lawsuits concerned forced sterilizations approved by the Alberta Eugenics Board before the Sexual Sterilization Act was repealed.
Alberta later abandoned the forced sterilization bill.
The Alberta Legislature passed Bill 202 in March 2000.
Bill 202 amended Alberta's Marriage Act to define marriage as between a man and a woman.
Bill 202 invoked the notwithstanding clause to shield the opposite-sex definition from Charter challenges.
A legislature can invoke the notwithstanding clause only for legislation it otherwise has authority to enact.
The Supreme Court of Canada's Reference re Same-Sex Marriage ruling was issued in 2004.
In that reference, the Supreme Court held that the definition of marriage falls within the exclusive authority of the Parliament of Canada.
The implication of that ruling was that Bill 202 was beyond the Alberta Legislature's constitutional powers.
The Alberta Legislature proposed Bill 2, the Back to School Act, in October 2025.
The Back to School Act used the notwithstanding clause to override sections 2 and 7 through 15.
The Back to School Act's override covered freedom of association.
Freedom of association has protected unions' right to strike since Saskatchewan Federation of Labour v Saskatchewan.
Alberta used the Back to School Act to order the Alberta Teachers' Association back to work.
The Alberta Teachers' Association had been on strike since early October 2025.
Some observers said Alberta's use of section 33 could encourage other provinces to invoke it in their own labour disputes.
In 2024, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith said she might invoke the clause to protect a ban on gender-affirming healthcare.
An Alberta bill introduced in November 2025 invoked the clause to protect a ban on gender-affirming healthcare.
The Supreme Court of Canada decided Vriend v Alberta in 1998.
Alberta considered invoking the clause after the Vriend decision.
Alberta Premier Ralph Klein resisted invoking the clause in response to Vriend.
On November 22, 2019, Education Minister Dominic Cardy introduced a bill in the New Brunswick Legislative Assembly.
Cardy's bill would have ended non-medical vaccination exemptions for schoolchildren.
Cardy's bill initially invoked the notwithstanding clause.
Cardy said the override was intended to pre-empt court and Charter challenges.
Cardy said an organized, well-financed lobby sought to derail efforts to protect vulnerable children.
The notwithstanding clause was removed from the New Brunswick bill in June 2020.
The New Brunswick bill was defeated at third reading.
The third-reading vote on the New Brunswick bill was a free vote.
Ontario passed the Better Local Government Act in August 2018.
The Act directed Toronto City Council to change its ward boundaries for the 2018 municipal election.
The Act required Toronto's wards to match federal and provincial electoral ridings.
The boundary change reduced Toronto's wards from 47 to 25.
Ontario Premier Doug Ford said Toronto City Council had failed to act on critical issues facing the city.
Ford claimed the change would save $25 million over four years.
The intent of the ward bill was controversial.
The timing of the ward bill was controversial because it came in the middle of a municipal election campaign.
Toronto's wards had already been realigned for the 2018 municipal election.
The earlier realignment expanded the number of Toronto wards from 44 to 47.
The earlier realignment consolidated several existing wards.
The earlier realignment added new wards.
On September 10, 2018, Superior Court Justice Edward Belobaba struck down the Better Local Government Act as unconstitutional.
Belobaba held that larger wards infringed voters' right to an election that provides effective representation.
Belobaba held that unilaterally changing ward boundaries during the campaign infringed candidates' freedom of expression.
Shortly after the ruling, Ford announced plans to introduce legislation invoking the notwithstanding clause to overcome it.
If Ford's proposed legislation had passed, it would have been Ontario's first use of the clause.
On September 19, 2018, the Court of Appeal for Ontario stayed Belobaba's decision.
The stay allowed Ontario to restore Toronto's 25-ward structure.
During oral argument on the stay, counsel for the attorney general said the government would abandon the override legislation if the stay was granted.
The Court of Appeal later overturned Belobaba's ruling after a full hearing.
The Court of Appeal's final decision was 3–2.
The Supreme Court of Canada upheld the Court of Appeal's ruling in 2021.
The Supreme Court's ruling on Toronto's wards was 5–4.
The Supreme Court majority held that the Better Local Government Act did not violate freedom of expression.
The Supreme Court majority held that the Act did not violate the unwritten constitutional principle of democracy.
Ontario passed the Protecting Ontario Elections Act, 2021, in early 2021.
The Act restricted private-sector organizations from running political advertisements outside election periods.
In June 2021, the Ontario Superior Court found that the advertising restrictions violated freedom of expression.
The Ontario Superior Court struck down the provisions imposing those restrictions.
Ontario then passed the Protecting Elections and Defending Democracy Act, 2021, to restore the restrictions using the notwithstanding clause.
In March 2023, the Court of Appeal for Ontario struck down the restrictions again.
The Court of Appeal ruled that the restrictions violated voter participation rights protected by section 3 of the Charter.
The Supreme Court of Canada affirmed the Court of Appeal's ruling in 2025.
The Supreme Court's decision on the political advertising restrictions was 5–4.
Ontario passed a bill concerning education workers on November 3, 2022.
The bill imposed a contract on Ontario education workers represented by the Canadian Union of Public Employees, or CUPE.
The imposed contract was intended to prevent the education workers from striking.
The bill invoked the notwithstanding clause to try to prevent a constitutional challenge by CUPE based on freedom of association.
The education workers went on strike despite the passage of the bill.
The Ontario government faced strong public backlash over the law.
Other unions threatened to walk off the job in solidarity.
Other unions threatened to protest the law in solidarity.
The backlash and threatened solidarity actions led the Ontario government to reach a deal with CUPE.
Ontario repealed the law under the deal.
The law's provisions were deemed never to have been in effect.
The law's penalties were deemed never to have been in effect.
CUPE ended the strike in exchange for repeal.
Contract negotiations resumed.
The Charter came into force in 1982.
After the Charter came into force, Quebec's Parti Québécois government passed the Act respecting the Constitution Act.
The Act inserted wording invoking section 33 into every law passed by the National Assembly of Quebec during the blanket application period.
The Act also retroactively amended every existing Quebec law to invoke section 33.
The blanket invocation was intended to shield all Quebec provincial laws from challenges.

question.text: A province passes a law in January 2027, but its notwithstanding declaration does not come into force until July 2027. If the declaration specifies no earlier expiry date and is not renewed, when does it expire?
options: In January 2032, five years after the law was passed.
In July 2032, five years after the declaration came into force.
At the first provincial election after the declaration comes into force, even if it occurs before July 2032.
Only when the province repeals the law, because the declaration specifies no expiry date.
